guide.title: Medication Safety & Error Prevention
guide.lead: Errors come from look-alike packs, decimal points, fatigue and rush. Organise the drug bag so the wrong drug is hard to grab, read every label aloud, calculate twice, and when something goes wrong, tell the truth quickly – the patient's safety and the next patient's depend on it.

sections.title: Error traps
rows: Tall-man lettering, separate storage, read aloud
Label in mg/mL; separate IM and IV stock
.5 mg read as 5 mg; 1.0 mg as 10 mg
Leading zero always (0.5 mg); never a trailing zero (1 mg)
Write "mcg" or "micrograms" in full, never µg
Closed-loop, two-person check for high-alert drugs

steps.title: Tell
steps.text: Medical direction and the receiving hospital, honestly and now.

steps.title: Record
steps.text: Accurate documentation and an incident report.

steps.title: Learn
steps.text: Debrief; fix the system (storage, labels, training).

quiz.q: After giving IM 'epinephrine', you notice the vial was ephedrine. The patient improved. You:
options: Notify medical direction and the hospital, document accurately, file an incident report

quiz.q: Morphine 4 mg ordered; vial 10 mg/mL. Draw up:
Dark nightclub; you gave 'naloxone' but nothing happened. The empty vial says ondansetron. Most likely?
quiz.explanation: Read labels aloud, even in the dark.

quiz.q: A partner hurriedly asks for 'epinephrine for the code'. Best safety step?
options: Read the label aloud with the concentration as you hand it over
Wait for them to fetch it

quiz.q: Correct way to write half a milligram:
Just culture response to an honest slip:
options: Console the person and fix the system

quiz.q: Unsure about a drug or dose:
options: Don't give it until you've checked
quiz.explanation: Ask a partner, medical direction or a reference.

options: Distinguish similar drug names (DOPamine vs DOBUTamine)

flashcards.question: Seven rights
flashcards.answer: Right patient, drug, dose, route, time, documentation, and the right to refuse.

flashcards.question: Look-alike, sound-alike drugs
flashcards.answer: Similar names or packs (epinephrine/ephedrine, dopamine/dobutamine). Separate them, use tall-man lettering, read aloud.

flashcards.question: Three-check system
flashcards.answer: When taking it out, when preparing, before giving – read the label aloud each time.

flashcards.question: After a medication error
flashcards.answer: Assess and treat the patient, tell medical direction and the hospital honestly, document, incident report, debrief and fix the system.

flashcards.question: Decimal danger
flashcards.answer: 0.1 mg vs 1 mg is tenfold. Always a leading zero, never a trailing zero. Volume = dose ÷ concentration; check with a partner.

flashcards.question: Just culture
flashcards.answer: Human error: console and fix the system. At-risk behaviour: coach. Reckless behaviour: discipline. Encourages reporting.

flashcards.question: High-alert medications
flashcards.answer: Opioids, sedatives, vasopressors (epinephrine), insulin, anticoagulants, concentrated electrolytes.

flashcards.question: Not sure about a drug?
flashcards.answer: Don't give it. Check with a partner, medical direction or a reference. "Let me check" is always acceptable.

critical.scenario: First week on the job: the drug bag is disorganised. Asked for oral glucose, you hand over a tube of lidocaine gel, which your partner squeezes into the patient's cheek before noticing.
critical.question: What now, and what failed?

options.t: Remove it, give the correct oral glucose, monitor; tell medical direction, document, report – and fix the bag layout and label-reading
Give glucagon instead without telling anyone

critical.explanation: Organised stock and reading aloud prevent most of these.
critical.kpi: Responds to a medication error and identifies system causes

critical.scenario: 68-year-old with chest pain; meds include metoprolol, lisinopril and tadalafil 'as needed', last taken 2 days ago. SpO₂ 93%.
critical.question: Which drugs are indicated, which contraindicated?

options.t: Aspirin chewed and oxygen to 94–98%; withhold nitroglycerin – tadalafil within 48 hours

options.f: That rule is for sildenafil; tadalafil is 48 hours.

critical.explanation: Ask about PDE-5 inhibitors by name; patients often don't mention them.

critical.scenario: 3 a.m., 6-year-old with severe asthma. Your tired partner draws up albuterol 5 mg instead of the protocol's 2.5 mg for this child; you notice before giving.
critical.question: What does this teach?

options.t: A near miss: give the correct dose now; afterwards debrief, use weight-based charts or the calculator, and two-person checks for children

options.f: This is human error: fix the system.

critical.explanation: Fatigue is a known error factor at night.
critical.kpi: Uses a near miss to improve medication safety
